rows.recommendation: Short-term MCS should be considered in patients with cardiogenic shock as a BTR, BTD, BTB. Further indications include treatment of the cause of cardiogenic shock or long-term MCS or transplantation.

IABP may be considered in patients with cardiogenic shock as a BTR, BTD, BTB, including treatment of the cause of cardiogenic shock (i.e. mechanical complication of acute MI) or long-term MCS or transplantation.
IABP is not routinely recommended in post-MI cardiogenic shock.

section_11.3.11_pre-discharge_assessment.main_message: Optimize treatment before discharge to relieve congestion and reduce readmission and mortality risk; continue or initiate guideline-directed oral medical therapy when appropriate.
key_points: A significant proportion of patients with AHF are discharged with minimal or no weight loss and persistent congestion; persistent congestion before discharge is associated with higher readmission and mortality risk (refs 427, 472).
Treatment including diuretic dose should be optimized to keep patient free of congestion (refs 426, 472).
In those admitted with ADHF, continue oral OMT except consider dose reduction/withdrawal for haemodynamic instability, severely impaired renal function, or hyperkalaemia.
Once haemodynamic stabilization is achieved with IV therapy, treatment should be optimized before discharge (ref 467).

Treatment optimization aims: (1) relieve congestion, (2) treat comorbidities such as iron deficiency that impact post-discharge outcome (ref 512), (3) initiate or restart oral OMT with beneficial effects on outcome. Doses may be uptitrated before discharge and/or early post-discharge.
Optimization of medical treatment is associated with lower 30-day readmission risk; prospective randomized trials limited to date (refs 103, 467, 513).
Retrospective analyses indicate discontinuation or dose reduction of beta-blocker therapy during AHF hospitalization is associated with worse outcomes (ref 514).
Initiation of ARNI in recently hospitalized stable patients with HFrEF, including those who are ACE-I/ARB naive, is safe and may be considered (refs 106, 107).
A prospective randomized trial showed benefit/safety with sotagliflozin in diabetic patients hospitalized for HF irrespective of LVEF (ref 136).
